title: From Silicon Valley of India to the Sea: The Bengaluru IT Couple Who Swam the Palk Strait
excerpt: Danish Abdi and Vrushali Prasade completed the 32-km crossing from Sri Lanka to India in under 11 hours, becoming the first couple to do it side by side
body:
They build software by day. On a cloudless morning in early May, they jumped into the sea.

Danish Abdi, a game designer, and Vrushali Prasade, an IT professional, are not the sort of people you would expect to find bobbing in the currents between two countries. The Bengaluru-based couple — known to their Instagram followers as the "Fit Couple" — have just completed something that most people would consider certifiably insane: a 32-kilometre open-water swim from Talaimannar, Sri Lanka to Dhanushkodi, Tamil Nadu, following the mythical route of Ram Setu.

They did it side by side, in 10 hours and 45 minutes, becoming the first Indian couple to swim the Palk Strait together.

## The Route of Legends

The Palk Strait, the narrow stretch of water separating the southern tip of India from Sri Lanka's northwest coast, is one of the most challenging open-water courses in Asia. Shallow enough in places that you can almost see the bottom — the remnants of what geologists call Adam's Bridge and what Hindu tradition knows as Ram Setu — but treacherous with its unpredictable currents, jellyfish, and sudden tidal shifts.

Danish and Vrushali chose the classic route: Talaimannar to Dhanushkodi, swimming northwest to southeast through waters that can range from deceptively calm to violently choppy within the same hour. The strait has claimed even experienced swimmers; completing it as a synchronised duo, maintaining pace with each other while battling different current forces on each side, adds a layer of complexity that solo crossings do not face.

## From Fear to the Finish Line

The most remarkable part of their story may be its beginning. Vrushali, by her own account, was once terrified of water. Not mildly uncomfortable — genuinely afraid of drowning. The transformation from hydrophobia to conquering one of Asia's most notorious maritime crossings is the kind of arc that would strain credulity in a screenplay.

The couple trained for months, gradually building endurance in pools and coastal waters around Bengaluru and Goa. Their preparation was methodical, reflecting the analytical mindset of their tech careers — tracking distances, monitoring heart rates, planning nutrition for a swim that would burn thousands of calories. Manipal Hospitals, which backed the crossing, provided medical support throughout the swim.

Videos of their crossing — Danish and Vrushali stroking through open water with the Sri Lankan coast disappearing behind them — went viral on Instagram, racking up millions of views and sparking a wave of admiration from India's growing adventure sports community.

## The Cultural Current

The Ram Setu route adds a layer of cultural significance that transcends the athletic achievement. The chain of limestone shoals between India and Sri Lanka has been a source of fascination, religious devotion, and political debate for centuries. In the Ramayana, it is the bridge built by Lord Rama's army to reach Lanka; in geological terms, it is a series of natural formations that were likely above sea level as recently as 500 years ago.

Swimming along this route — literally following the path of mythology — resonates powerfully in a country where the Ramayana remains a living cultural text. For the diaspora, the symbolism is even richer: two modern Indians, working in global technology, choosing to test themselves against a challenge that connects India's ancient narrative tradition with contemporary endurance sport.

## The Bigger Picture

Danish and Vrushali join a small but growing roster of Indian endurance athletes who are pushing the boundaries of what the country's sporting culture considers normal. Until recently, Indian sport was narrowly defined by cricket, with occasional bursts of attention for hockey, badminton, or athletics during Olympic years. The emergence of open-water swimmers, ultramarathoners, and adventure athletes represents a quiet cultural shift — one driven largely by urban professionals with the means and motivation to pursue extreme challenges.

The Palk Strait has seen increasing traffic from Indian swimmers in recent years. In 2023, autistic teenager Haresh Barath Mohan completed the crossing, while Delhi University student Kamya Bhardwaj set a record for a non-stop return swim. Danish and Vrushali's achievement as a couple adds a new chapter to this growing tradition.

For NRI tech workers — the kind who know Bengaluru as both their professional launching pad and their permanent emotional anchor — the story of the Fit Couple hits close to home. It is a reminder that India's most interesting sporting stories are increasingly being written not in stadiums but in open water, on mountain trails, and across deserts, by people who refuse to accept that a desk job defines the limits of what they can do.
